title: What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, is an architecture that retrieves relevant information from an external knowledge source and supplies that evidence to a language model as context before the model generates an answer. RAG can improve factual grounding, make private or frequently changing knowledge available to the model, and provide sources that can be cited without retraining the language model.

title: Core RAG Pipeline
text: A typical RAG pipeline has several stages: ingest documents, split or chunk them, create searchable representations, retrieve candidates for a user query, optionally rerank the candidates, construct a prompt containing the best evidence, generate an answer with an LLM, and evaluate or trace the result. Retrieval and generation should be measured separately because either stage can fail independently.

title: Evaluating Retrieval Quality
text: Retrieval quality in RAG systems is commonly measured with ranking metrics such as Recall at K, Precision at K, Mean Reciprocal Rank, and nDCG. Recall at K measures whether relevant evidence was found in the top K results, Precision at K measures how much of the returned set is relevant, MRR emphasizes the rank position of the first relevant result, and nDCG rewards relevant documents appearing near the top.

title: BM25 Lexical Retrieval
text: BM25 is a lexical ranking method based on term frequency, document frequency, and document length normalization. It is strong when exact words, product names, identifiers, acronyms, or rare terms in the query also occur in relevant documents. Lexical retrieval does not require neural embeddings.

title: Dense Semantic Retrieval
text: Dense retrieval encodes queries and documents as numeric vectors using an embedding model. Similarity search can retrieve semantically related text even when the query and document use different vocabulary. Dense retrieval is useful for paraphrases and conceptual similarity but may miss exact identifiers that lexical retrieval handles well.

title: Hybrid Retrieval
text: Hybrid retrieval combines lexical methods such as BM25 with dense vector similarity. Lexical retrieval is strong for exact terms and identifiers, while dense retrieval captures semantic similarity. A common design normalizes both score types and fuses them with configurable weights before optional reranking.

title: FAISS Vector Search
text: FAISS is an open-source library for efficient similarity search over dense vectors. For normalized embeddings, inner-product search can be used to rank vectors similarly to cosine similarity. A FAISS index can be built once for a stable corpus and rebuilt when the corpus or embedding model changes.

title: SentenceTransformers Embeddings
text: SentenceTransformers provides pretrained embedding models that convert sentences and passages into dense vectors. In a RAG system, the same embedding model should normally encode both corpus passages and incoming queries so they can be compared in the same vector space.

title: CrossEncoder Reranking
text: A CrossEncoder jointly scores a query and candidate document pair and is commonly used as a second-stage reranker. Because it evaluates each pair together, it can be more accurate than bi-encoder similarity but is more computationally expensive. It is therefore usually applied only to a short candidate list produced by BM25, dense search, or hybrid retrieval.

title: Document Chunking
text: RAG systems often split long documents into smaller chunks before embedding. Chunks should be large enough to preserve useful context but small enough to retrieve specific evidence. Chunk size, overlap, headings, and metadata can all affect retrieval quality, and the best configuration should be evaluated rather than assumed.

title: Grounded Generation
text: Grounded generation constrains an LLM to answer from retrieved evidence rather than relying freely on unsupported model knowledge. A robust prompt should require citations, forbid unsupported claims, and instruct the model to state when the retrieved evidence is insufficient.

title: Local LLM Serving
text: A local instruction-tuned language model can generate RAG answers without paid APIs. Model weights are downloaded once and cached locally. When the application starts, the model is loaded into CPU or GPU memory; when the application stops, the model no longer consumes runtime memory.

title: Citation Validation
text: Citation validation checks that source identifiers cited by an answer actually exist in the retrieved context. Citation validity and citation coverage are different metrics: validity measures whether citations point to allowed sources, while coverage measures whether factual answer claims are accompanied by citations.

title: Groundedness Evaluation
text: Groundedness evaluation estimates whether claims in a generated answer are supported by retrieved evidence. Methods range from lexical overlap and embedding similarity to natural-language-inference models and LLM judges. Heuristic scores should be labeled clearly because they are not equivalent to human verification.

title: Abstention and Insufficient Evidence
text: A reliable RAG assistant should abstain when retrieved evidence is insufficient. An abstention is different from a hallucination: a statement that the system lacks enough evidence should not be penalized as an unsupported factual answer if the system is correctly refusing to invent information.

title: RAG Observability
text: RAG observability records the query, retrieved documents, retrieval and reranker scores, generated answer, citations, latency, model version, and evaluation signals for each request. Query-level traces help diagnose failures that aggregate metrics can hide.

title: Latency in RAG Systems
text: End-to-end RAG latency can be decomposed into retrieval, reranking, prompt construction, and generation time. Local language-model generation is often the dominant cost, while vector retrieval over a small corpus may take only milliseconds. Recording stage-level latency makes bottlenecks visible.

title: SQLite for Local RAG Tracing
text: SQLite is a lightweight embedded database that requires no separate server. A local RAG application can store query traces, answers, retrieved sources, metrics, and latency in a SQLite file and later export those records for dashboards or analysis.

title: RAG Failure Modes
text: Common RAG failure modes include retrieval misses, poor ranking, incomplete context, contradictory sources, fabricated citations, unsupported answer claims, excessive latency, and answering when the evidence is insufficient. Evaluation should identify which stage caused a failure rather than treating all bad answers as generation errors.

title: Why Evaluate Answerable and Unanswerable Queries
text: A useful RAG evaluation set should contain both answerable and intentionally unanswerable questions. Answerable questions test whether retrieval and generation can use available evidence. Unanswerable questions test whether the system can recognize missing evidence and abstain instead of hallucinating.
